description: USDA grant-domain terminology for regenerative agriculture: soil-health vocabulary, common funder language, key concept disambiguations. Drawn from USDA NRCS, SARE, and AFRI program materials. Starter pack — expand as field experience accumulates.

domains.name: Soil health practices
domains.description: USDA-NRCS canonical soil-health vocabulary: cover crops, no-till, crop diversity, livestock integration, perennial systems.

domains.name: Common funder language
domains.description: Phrases USDA, SARE, and AFRI reviewers expect to see — outcome metrics, evaluation framing, theory-of-change vocabulary.

domains.name: Concept disambiguation
domains.description: Distinctions reviewers care about — regenerative vs. organic vs. sustainable, conservation vs. restoration, etc.

facts.statement: USDA-NRCS canonical five soil-health principles: (1) minimize soil disturbance, (2) maximize soil cover, (3) maximize biodiversity, (4) maximize presence of living roots, (5) integrate livestock. Used as the structural rubric for cover-crops + no-till + grazing applications.

USDA cover-crop categorization: cool-season legumes (clovers, vetches), cool-season grasses (rye, wheat), warm-season legumes (cowpea, sunn hemp), warm-season grasses (sorghum-sudangrass), brassicas (radish, mustard). Mix selection drives N-fixation, soil structure, and grazing-window outcomes.

USDA distinguishes no-till (zero soil disturbance, residue undisturbed) from strip-till (narrow tilled strip with residue between rows) from reduced-till (one or two passes). Practice code 329 covers all three. Soil-health scoring favors no-till > strip-till > reduced-till.

USDA-NRCS Soil Health Assessment uses SOM (soil organic matter) percentage as a primary indicator. Baseline by region varies (1-3% typical for degraded cropland in temperate US); 0.1-0.3% annual increase under regenerative practice is a credible 5-year outcome claim. Avoid uncited >1%/yr claims — reviewers flag.

Adaptive Multi-Paddock (AMP) grazing, Mob grazing, and Management-Intensive Grazing (MIG) are the canonical USDA-recognized rotational systems. AMP is the most evidence-supported in peer-reviewed soil-health literature; cite Teague et al. and Stanley et al. for outcome claims.

USDA / SARE reviewers reward outcome statements ('30 producers adopt cover crops on 1,200 acres by 2028') over input statements ('we will host 10 workshops'). Frame every objective as a verifiable change in producer behavior, acreage, soil indicator, or income — not activity completed.

USDA AFRI Foundational reviewers expect a Theory of Change: inputs → activities → outputs → outcomes → impact. The transition from outputs (workshops held) to outcomes (acres converted) to impact (water-quality / soil-carbon shift) is where most weak proposals collapse. Quantify each transition.

USDA programs (VAPG, REAP, BFRDP) score cash match higher than in-kind match even when ratio is identical. In-kind labor must be valued at independent-living wage rates; cite the rate source. Federal funds cannot be used as match (except Indian Self-Determination Act § 104(C)).

USDA distinguishes Organic (NOP-certified, prohibited-substance compliance), Sustainable (broad term, no certification), and Regenerative (no federal cert; ROC and Land to Market are the recognized third-party schemes). Reviewers flag conflation. Use 'regenerative' for soil-building practice claims, 'organic' only for NOP-certified parcels.

USDA Conservation (NRCS practices: maintain or improve current resource condition) is distinct from Restoration (NRCS Restoration Practice Standards: reverse degradation, often wetland or grassland). EQIP funds primarily conservation; CRP funds restoration via 10-15-year contracts. Project framing should match program intent.

USDA Specialty Crop Block Grant Program (SCBGP) defines specialty crops as: fruits, vegetables, tree nuts, dried fruits, horticulture, nursery crops, floriculture. Specifically excludes: corn, soybeans, wheat, rice, cotton, peanuts, hay, livestock, dairy. Mushrooms are eligible (specialty crop). Maple syrup is eligible as horticulture product.

USDA VAPG defines value-added as one of: (1) physical change (e.g., milk → cheese), (2) production segregation (e.g., grass-fed beef), (3) physical bundling (e.g., CSA boxes), (4) marketing for renewable energy. Producers must own the agricultural product through value-add — third-party processors do not qualify. Match must be 1:1 cash + in-kind.

relationships.description: The five principles' 'maximize soil cover' principle is operationalized via the cover-crop categorization.
The five principles' 'minimize disturbance' principle is operationalized via the no-till practice spectrum.
The five principles' 'integrate livestock' principle is operationalized via AMP / Mob / MIG grazing systems.
Outcome-vs-input framing is the proximate component of a defensible Theory of Change logic model.
VAPG value-added claims for 'regenerative beef' or 'regenerative dairy' must use 'regenerative' precisely — not interchangeably with organic — or reviewers may flag for substantiation.
